text: VAT is an indirect tax , basically its the government sort of hiding another form of taxation , the companies that charge it are just the middle men ( Tax collectors !) , they can also claim back VAT they have to pay for goods , so they can be tax neutral , but the ultimate payer is of course the consumer or anyone no VAT registered  .  VAT will always go up , and more companies and individuals pushed into be VAT registered . UK for most goods is now 20% , in Japan it was 5% then 8% and now 10% , better get used to it unfortunately.  The US now has Trumps tariffs on a lot of imports , which I believe a lot of Americans don't understand , is not paid by the exporting country , as Trump would have them believe, but by the US importer , who, drum roll, passes it onto the consumer , so actually US citizens are the ones paying the tariff not the exporting country !

author: @AvidGardener5D
text: My tip is, never be a tourist, always be a local.  Don't talk to anyone you don't know on the street. Know where you are going by researching ahead of time.  Pay in cash.  Don't walk around looking bewildered. Look determined, like you have a goal in mind.  If you have to stop, don't stop in the middle of the street, stop somewhere where there's a wall behind you so you can look at your phone or whatever without giving someone an opportunity to take you by surprise. Don't clutch tourist articles, put them in your bag.  You're a local, remember?  Stay sober in public.   I've lived in major cities and traveled around the world and this has always served me well.

text:
Thanks Cal. I'm going to Asia next year, definitely going to hit Bangkok, Pattaya, and Hong Kong. Thought about Vietnam. I may or may not go. It depends on my timing, but this was informative. 

It's really nothing different than any other developing country: same scams, different faces, different language, that's all.

All those people who are being turned off by traveling to Vietnam, you're going to face the same in every country. First world countries, third world countries. If you're a savvy and wary traveler, you'll see it coming from a mile away. It's up to you how vulnerable you are.

The best thing about most Asian countries is there's not really any violence. You're not getting straight up robbed. You're being tricked. Being tricked is on you. Being strong-armed is a different thing entirely and that very rarely happens in most Asian countries.

People are completely misinterpreting Cal’s video and confusing opportunistic hassle with actual danger. Every region in the world has a tourist tax; you just need to understand what kind of tax you are dealing with. 

There is a huge  difference between strong-arm crime and cons/scams, and understanding this distinction is the difference between traveling safely and staying home out of irrational fear.

1. The High-Risk Zone: Strong-Arm Crime (The Caribbean / Parts of Latin America)In places with high rates of violent crime, like parts of Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, or various major hubs in the Americas, crime is often predatory and physical (strong-arm). 

This means armed robberies, physical muggings, or targeted smash-and-grabs.
The Tactic: Criminals leverage physical dominance, weapons, and environmental isolation to force compliance.The Reality: If you get cornered in a bad neighborhood or set up by a predatory taxi driver in these zones, spatial awareness won't save you. 

You cannot outsmart a gun or a blade. Your only defensive move is compliance—handing over your wallet and hoping you don't get hurt.

2. The Low-Violent Zone: Psychological Exploitation (Vietnam, Thailand, Egypt) 
By contrast, violent crime against tourists in Southeast Asia or Egypt is statistically incredibly rare. Instead, you face hyper-aggressive opportunism and psychological traps.

The Tactic: These scammers weaponize your own psychology against you. They exploit your politeness, your desire to avoid a public scene, your lack of spatial awareness, and your ignorance of local currency/pricing.

The Reality: An Egyptian vendor placing a "free gift" in your hand or the pyramids are closed and only they can grant you access or give you a ride around on a camel for a ridiculous price that you didn't negotiate beforehand, or a Vietnamese restaurant pulling a "switcheroo menu" isn’t trying to assault you. 

They are playing a high-pressure mental game, betting that you will pay a fake $40 bill just to escape the social awkwardness.

The Golden Rule: Scams are 95% Preventable

You cannot outthink a violent strong-arm mugger, but you can absolutely outsmart a scammer. 

In Asia, your safety is rarely at risk, but your wallet always is—meaning the power is entirely in your hands. You can completely avoid paying the "scam tax" by being hyper-aware and proactive:

Audit the Paper Trail: Take photos of the menu and prices before you order. If they bring a duplicate menu with jacked-up prices at the end of the meal, you have digital receipts to kill the argument instantly.

Kill the Cash Flash: Do not walk around with large rolls of cash or flashy gold jewelry. No one in Hanoi or Bangkok is impressed by a Rolex, but it does signal to pickpockets that you are a high-value, low-awareness target.

Lock Down Your Identity: Leave your physical passport locked securely in your hotel room. Carry a Xerox copy or a digital scan on your phone for daily use.

Bypass the Street Hustle: Never flag down random street taxis or tuk-tuks. Use localized apps like Grab where the route is GPS-tracked, the driver is identified, and the price is locked before you even step inside.Stop letting Cal’s video scare you out of traveling. 

Western Europe has pickpockets, the Caribbean has strong-arm crime, and Asia has scammers. The beautiful thing about an Asian scam is that if you do an hour of research, keep your wits about you, and shed your fear of being impolite, you are effectively untouchable.

I wanted to add that I live in Times Square, 42nd and 9th Avenue, and I see the scammers every day. I have a family friend who's an undercover cop and literally all he does is walk around and let people pickpocket him. He's in disguise sort of and arrests people daily doing that.

Then I see people who get scammed by the rickshaw drivers or they don't realize the price, how much it is. Some of them, you go around the block and it's $150 and you can't argue it. They'll put the price clearly marked on the side of their cart of the rickshaw and people don't really pay attention that it's $2.50 a minute or $5 a minute or more.

Or the people dressed up as your favorite Marvel characters or a giant gorilla, a Transformer, you give them your phone to take a picture. Unless you give them $5 or more, they won't give you your phone back. If you just happen to take a picture near them or maybe of them, they will insist that you give them money. They will literally try to intimidate you and they will surround you because they got each other's backs. They won't let off until they either see the police coming or you give them money.

Never give them your cell phone to take a picture. Never do that.

text: The "down on his luck xpat" scam hit me up at BKK, he was moping around and mumbling, the scooter out of gas scam in HCMC, she rode up and was crying and had some story, I gave her 22 dong, sometimes I just give a few dong to see a response. Haven't had the phone taking peeps try anything yet but some locals warned me about holding my phone to openly while on the back of a grab. The pickpocket scam is something I didn't think was in HCMC, yet or as widespread like the EU. Just use your wits and watch your drink, never take a free drink. The BV walking street is just a sad commentary on shitty tourism, walk fast once but there are so many other areas you can go to, it's too loud and it's all a scam. Do yourself a favor and avoid it.

text:
The streets you just walk across, don't stop, you don't even have to look both ways just go. No one will hit you unless you back up or stop. To pick up a kitten, walk into the street with arms up and start to wave them as you are preparing to stop. Stand up and face direction you intend to walk and start walking. It's a lot of fun to cross the street there. :)

Vietnam is one of the best places to visit on earth. People are the nicest and crime is very low. It is clean and you can learn so much on the history. Just watch for the swarms of kids, they will reach in your pockets in some areas so keep it zipped up.

Keep up the awesome work!!!

text:
Very interesting how people in northern Vietnam/Hanoi are camera shy and borderline rude/hostile about being filmed. 
I get that not everyone wants to be filmed...privacy, busy, having a lousy day etc. Not everyone wants to be on the internet...and not everyone knows or cares that you are a big, famous YouTuber with a massive following...but you took it in your stride, with good humour. We even got to hear Sonny try to negotiate with the security lady in Vietnamese. She doesnt know that you are her brother-in-law and should treat you nicer 😂😅.
Anyway, despite the challenges, thanks for showing us all the candid angles and perspectives...the different reception you sometimes get in these places. We appreciate it.
#Balance.

author: @SubEveryLanguage
text: In Vietnam, you don't necessarily need to seek out Michelin-starred restaurants. Instead, look for local eateries. At these places, you will enjoy food of equal or even superior quality, but at a significantly lower price. Vietnam has no shortage of talented chefs who can cook dishes on par with those at Michelin-starred establishments. The main difference is that Michelin restaurants are more famous, meticulously organized, have stricter hygiene standards, and feature nicer decor. In short, you are paying for the peripheral dining experience rather than just the food itself. My advice is to find local spots frequented by everyday residents, rather than places that are just famous on the internet

Yes, the image in English means ''Born to drift free” Similar to other familiar names the top-of-the-line electric motorcycle is the Vinfast Viper and when associated with Da Nang city and Hoi An ancient town creates a poetic parallel image. It reflects both the free-spiritedness of a young, modern city and the tranquil rhythm of an ancient heritage site.
- Modern Da Nang: A city of bridges, beaches, and a dynamic pace of life, always looking towards the future.
- Ancient Hoi An: An ancient town with lanterns, moss-covered tiled roofs, where memories and culture are preserved.
- The spirit of freedom: On one side, a constantly moving flow; on the other, a stillness that remains open to the world.
This combination makes the phrase “Born to drift free” a powerful and evocative message: both an invitation to tourists and an affirmation of the identity of this Central Vietnamese region I LOVE VIETNAM FORM DA NANG CITY AND HOI AN ANCIENT.

author: @MindfulAging-d9f
text:
Great choice starting with the giant Bánh Bao Thọ Phát! It's a fun, modern take on a classic and definitely a smart way to rack up the bill for the challenge.

What's fascinating about Saigon is that the expensive street food experience often isn't about super-sizing. It's about finding the small, unassuming spots that specialize in one dish but use premium, hyper-local ingredients—where the higher price reflects heritage and ingredient quality, not just quantity. It’s a totally different path to that $100 goal.

This distinction between getting a big meal versus a truly premium one at the street level is a focus of my own food explorations.

video_title: Vietnam's Stunning Imperial City (Hue in 1 Day)
author: @elepfly
text: The building with vibrant colors that you love is actually reconstructed recently as the original palace was destroyed completely during the war. As you can see, the weather in Hue is extremely hot and humid, so all of the color pigments will soon deteriorate, and the buildings then become just gray and brown which makes it look much older than it is, just like what you think of Khai Dinh's tomb. However, you can imagine a Hue citadel in its golden age, with all of those palaces, temples, and tombs all painted and ornated in a yellow, red, and blue theme of colors.

video_title: Vietnam's Stunning Imperial City (Hue in 1 Day)
author: @letsmadventure
text: That makes so much more sense haha. I was wondering how many of the buildings in the citadel were still so vibrant! It is really cool to get to see it as it looked back in its prime though, but I definitely also enjoy the faded look of Khai Dinh's tomb where you can really see the history. It is so special that we get to see both in Hue! Thanks so much for the info!

author: @samyak123456789
text:
Thanks for sharing this. We are about to visit Vietnam, and I have always been interested in history, especially Ho Chi Minh, Vietnam’s struggle for independence, and the suffering its people went through during different periods of foreign occupation and war.

I am glad you also showed the darker side of that history by visiting the prison. These places are painful, but they are important because they show what people endured and how those experiences shaped a nation.

Every country has dark chapters. Colonial powers often came in the name of trade, administration or religion, but in many places local people lost their land, freedom and lives. Today, many countries openly preserve those stories through museums, prisons and memorials.

India has equally painful stories. The Cellular Jail in the Andaman Islands is only one example, where prisoners suffered brutal punishment, isolation, forced labour and terrible conditions. There are also accounts of prisoners being left in remote and dangerous places with almost no chance of survival. These stories deserve to be preserved and told openly.

What I find difficult to understand is that when India strongly talks about its own colonial suffering, it is sometimes quickly labelled as propaganda or nationalism.

Remembering history does not mean hating people today, and it does not mean rejecting Western culture. There is nothing wrong with learning from the West or appreciating its culture. The problem is when we follow it so blindly that we become uncomfortable talking about what colonial powers once did to our own people.

I saw something similar in Korea, where museums and preserved villages openly show the suffering people faced during the Japanese occupation. Vietnam does the same. Many countries do. So why should India feel uncomfortable doing the same?

We can respect people today while still being honest about history. Preserving painful history is not hatred or propaganda. It is about respecting those who suffered and making sure future generations understand what happened. That is the hypocrisy I struggle to understand.

The question I often ask is: *why are we comfortable learning about the darkest chapters of other countries, but sometimes uncomfortable talking openly about our own?*

text:
Sir, you will enjoy William Dalrymple’s books . He is a world renowned historian living in Delhi. One of his books The Golden Road covers the spread of Buddhist and Hindu cultures in South East Asia.  It also talks about Champa and the influence of the dynasties in South India- the Pallavas, Cholas, and Chalukya. The great Khamir empire whose capital city was called Yashodharapura now known as Angkor which also has the world’s largest Hindu temple complex AngkorWat - present day Cambodia. 
The world Angkor comes from Nokor in Khamir which is the root of nagar in Sanskrit. Khamir kings were Hindus .
You will absolutely have an unbelievable experience in covering Angkor Wat. - it takes several days to cover such a massive complex.
Hope reading Dalrymple’s books will inspire you to explore regions and stories not yet explored by you.

text: Thank you for this week’s video, Harish. I so enjoy the history videos, and loved the ones when you explored about the wars. I think this is a good topic and fascinating, but the story didn’t fully come through. I think I understand the Champa community (which was new to me), that they are like the Nonya communities in Singapore and Malaysia, and have a unique culture. I miss more food-aligned blogs, as they bring me closer to India. The lunch clip did need to be a little longer, and better explained. While I don’t mind veg or non-veg food blogs, I think it could have been to cool to also explore Vietnam’s veg culture, and why there are restaurants dedicated to it and similarly Indian restaurants. I thought it was a good episode but I did skip a little bit of the history portion as it was a little repetitive and could have gone deeper beyond the museum like you did with the war one to explore the Champa community or shown the dance performances. Looking forward to the next one, Nidhi

author: @slybrookbuster1875
text: 1967-68 I walked up and down both sides of the Hai Van Pass on Road Mine Sweeps.  The Pass back then, was just as beautiful but very deadly.  In October 1967 we took over an ARVN combat base at the next pass on Highway One at north end of Lang Co Bay.  From there we ran mine road sweep north to Phu Loc just south of Phu Bai.  In December 1967 we move to the south side of Hai Van Pass to the Esso Plant and Nam O Bridge on the Da Nang side.  From the south side, we also did the same mine road sweeps to the top of the Pass. We lost people to mines and ambushes on both sides of the Pass.  Back then the railroad bridge in Nam O serviced both the RR, which was not in use and road traffic on Highway One. There used to be a beautiful solid marble turtle monument on the last turn on the north side overlooking Lang Co. The marble tablet on top of the turtle told the story about the longevity and hardship of building the railroad around the Pass. It was all written in French.  I believe that the North Vietnamese Army probably blew it off the turtle when they took over South Vietnam in 1975.  I have seen photos of it without the marble tablet on its back.      Thank you for the memories.  Golf 2/7 Marines, Vietnam.

Hi guys, Love your videos on Vietnam North to South.
My wife and I, we are in our late fifties early sixties, are travelling to Vietnam for the first time, after holidaying in Koh Samui Thailand for the past 9 years, in early June for 20 days, staying in Hanoi for a total of 4 nights then heading to Hoi An for a total of 15 nights. author: @388_days
text:
We are learning a lot about the history of Vietnam, which is not really taught in America schools. I picked up a couple of books so I could learn a bit about the history before we visited. I didn’t realize how many different groups of people inhabited the area we now know as Vietnam and how many battles were fought to control the land. I was also very surprised to learn that the Cham people were Hindu but later many turned to the Muslim faith. As we travel around we are humbled by how little we know about much of the world. Hopefully we will see peaceful times ahead for Vietnam and its neighbors. The people are so kind and respectful. 

-Chris

author: @Dunleap
text:
-flushable wet wipes.
- If you are a man, and do not expect access to Washing machine, take as many t-shirts as days you plan to travel. Go for cotton avoid polyester, when sweaty it smell bad, even taxi driver didn't know that I know what "hôi nách" mean -.- Bring antiperspirant, even in the winter.
- if you don not favour sea food, grab some dry snaks for long car trips, to always have something you like. Food in Vietnam is great, but in some areas they eat stuff that do not look appetizing, after long drive.  
- If going to Hanoi or other big city, and you have a beard. Get yourself a nice face mask that fit you well. Unfortunately, city air is not the best and your nose will be packed with stuff at the end of the day. If you don't like that, get a nice face mask. They sell them everywhere in vietnam, but if you are big head european fiding right size might be harder.

text:
That "leave the shoes for the sandal" process for the bathroom wasn't around when I was living and working in VN but it makes sense.  Those sandals are in that area and are not walked on the gravel so they're cleaner than your shoes.  Vietnamese people leave shoes and sandals at the door and walk barefoot in the house which I agree as much cleaner than us American wearing shoes in our home.  I think it's filthy how we wear our shoes in the house, put them on our couch, etc.

As for the caves, those are beautiful and really look surreal with the external sunlight beaming inside.

text: Don’t believe all of these fake social media influencers and lying YouTube posts who make Vietnam look like the hot new paradise on earth because it isn’t.  Just went to visit Vietnam and check it out and it’s a 6 out of 10.  Thailand is much better 9/10 for many reasons like much better infrastructure, the politeness of the local Thai people.  In Vietnam the vibe is more aggressive & rude like back in America and the language barrier is worse than you think so you can’t communicate with the people.  Plus the big elephant sitting in the living room is the stigma of the horrible Vietnam war dead ghosts still hangs where 58,000 Americans died and 3 million Vietnamese died gives it a weird paranormal feeling.  Reminded me of the killing fields of Cambodia with pol pot who killed 3 million of his own people or visiting world war 2 battlefields in Europe where millions were murdered with the same weird ghost paranormal feelings.  In Vietnam it was a constant surreal experience & feeling to think that my uncle fought only 49 miles from our beach front resort in Da Nang in one of the bloodiest battles of the Vietnam war where thousand perished in bloody door to door combat.  I couldn’t stop thinking about it and remembering his stories of almost being killed by a booby trap bomb toy bear he picked up and exploded in his face placed by the enemy.

text:
Hi…by using your tourist visa yes, you can search for a job, but you CANNOT legally work on a Tourist Visa. 

If you enter on a Tourist Visa to search for jobs locally:
1. Attend interviews and sign the employment agreement in Vietnam.
2. Employer processes your Work Permit documents locally.  
3. Do a quick "Visa Run" (fly/bus to neighboring Cambodia, Thailand, or Laos) to switch from Tourist Visa to your new Work Visa, then re-enter Vietnam.

author: @D4FChennel
text:
I’ve been spending a lot of time in Vietnam, and honestly, this video doesn’t really match my experience.

Of course scams exist — just like anywhere. I’ve taken taxis, bought things at markets and shops, and sometimes noticed different prices. But I usually check a few places first, get an idea of the normal price, and then decide. Once you know roughly what something should cost, it’s not difficult to avoid being overcharged.

For me, Vietnam feels like a very safe place overall. I’ve spent a lot of time here and have had overwhelmingly normal, friendly interactions with people.

I think there’s a big difference between saying “scams happen in Vietnam” and making it sound like Vietnam is full of scammers. The first is true; the second doesn’t match my experience at all.

text:
There's so many different scams, here as in many other countries. Personally I've had a very "friendly" Grab driver who in the end planned to dump me in a crocodile farm after robbing me. Buying cigarettes by street vendors around 75% more expensive. Scales at local markets 
weighing 10-15% wrong. Oranges injected with sugar solution. The shoe shine guys, another Grab driver trying to snatch my phone. An old woman trying to sell a banana pancake for 100.000 dong. And so on. It's a never ending story. Yet I've been living here for almost 6 years now and wouldn't want to be anywhere else. Because most people are really friendly and curious and want to interact. Crimes of course do happen but they are solved in a rapid pace. And obviously not all taxi drivers are scammers. I once dropped my phone, essential for me to survive, in a taxi in HCMC. After 10 minutes he returned where he dropped me off with my phone and completely refused the money I wanted to give him.

author: @hmmob3956
text:
Scam 5 is pretty common. I visited Vietnam recently and both in Hanoi and Saigon they tried this on me. I let it go because it was not a significant amount, but going forward I will simply ignore the aunties. 

1) Aunty walked towards me and offered me a free pastry ball (tasted actually pretty good, it was dry and old, but it was good). I asked how much. She said 30k, so I said yes, gave her 200k and she did not return enough change and said (after I asked) the price was 80k for 5 of the pastry balls, which obviously is overpriced. Clearly, she lied. As it turned out, she only returned 110k effectively charging 90k. In any case, I let it go. It was my first evening in Hanoi and I did not want to get upset.

2) Bought some fruit and similarly to 1) after I paid 100k for fruit that was supposed to cost 85k, I only received 5k with the aunty then saying the total was 95k. Again, too small of an amount to bother. The fruit was actually pretty good (in particular the bananas). 

In any case, I will have pen and paper with me and will be exceedingly careful if at all I ever buy from street aunties in Vietnam. And I will carry small denomination bills so that I can pay exactly what was agreed upon after taking possession of the products first. But, to be honest, to the most part I will not bother and ignore those cute aunties. Love Vietnam, but this reflects poorly on the country.

text:
I am in Vietnam at the moment, for the third time. I agree with a lot of what is said here, except for the weather.

Vietnam in winter is very cold in the north, it gets warmer as you go south. But Hanoi is very cold, don't come in the winter expecting tropical temperatures.

Danang is warmer but still not very hot in winter.

Stick to Nha Trang and further south if you want really tropical weather in the winter.

I truly admire and love him.

author: @ndkhoa2812
text:
There are two major beef Pho styles in Vietnam
Northern style (think Ha Noi):
+ The original style. But can mostly be found only within Vietnam, quite rare in the South and even rarer oversea
+ The broth is much clearer and a bit mild compare to Southern style. Making the broth clear requires some serious techniques!
+ Thinner noodle
+ More spring onion. Less brown/white onion
+ Dough stick (youtiao) is a standard side dish. NO vegetable & herb side dish
+ Table condiments: pickle garlic, chili paste (very finely grounded chili in vinegar, mostly homemade) & fresh chili. NO hoisin.

Southern style (think Sai Gon (or Ho Chi Minh city)): 
+ The most popular style outside of Vietnam. The majority of Pho in the US & Australia are Southern style. I find Australian version of Pho is much closer to the Vietnamese version than in the US.
+ The broth is richer, sweeter and more cloudy
+ Thicker noodle
+ Less spring onion. More brown/white onion
+ NO dough stick. Generous amount of vegetable & herb side dish
+ Table condiments: Hoisin, chili sauce (mostly off-the-shelf product), chili oil & fresh chili

Other notes:
- Phở Gà (Chicken Pho) is considered to be a completely different dish: The broth is made from chicken bone (not beef), using minimal amount of anise & cinnamon, but more ginger & shallot. Results in a very clear, more aromatic but less herby broth compare to the beef Pho. Lime leaves (shredded) is a MUST and give Phở Gà its unique aroma and taste. In Vietnam, a proper Pho shop will NOT sell Beef Pho and Chicken Pho together. Chicken Pho is a Northern specialty, most owners of Chicken Pho shop in the South are Northern immigrants
- Phở Thìn (@8:27) is not traditional and has its own unique style: using stir-fried beef instead of raw/cooked beef, results in a very smoky & rich, somewhat oily flavour. And yes, an insane amount of spring onion.
- It's hard to believe but you won't find any Sriracha sauce (yes, that famous rooster bottle!) in any Pho shop in Vietnam. In fact, most Vietnamese do not know about its existence.

I’m a Vietnamese and this is my comment about the Vietnamese ‘Phở’.
There are signification different of Phở among 3 locations, Phở in North Vietnam (Hanoi), South Vietnam (Saigon) and Phở in the United States and the world.
Phở in North Vietnam (Hanoi): The flavor is the best, but the taste is the worst due to lack of Beef Bones.
Phở in South Vietnam (Saigon): The flavor is not smell good as in North Vietnam but the taste is much better.
Phở in the United States and the world: The flavor is not smell good as in North Vietnam, and the taste is acceptable just because ‘fast foods McDonald cooking style’ instead of ‘family cooking’.

text:
I met a Vietnamese retired lawyer man and his family in 1994 in San Jose, but this story happened during an annual business training in Daytona, FL.  His family invited me in private beside business functions in that week. 
When we started to eat their food, I asked the ingredients and food processes, so he DIDN'T bother to explain the details of the ingredients and the rest (he talked a lot in general and we were hungry, so it would take a long time😂), so he just said:

text:
Beautiful? I was just in Hoi An and it has become a total dump and the food was overpriced and terrible. There was trash all along the Old Quarter lake and all of the street lamps were flat on the ground which not only looked ridiculous, but it presented a huge safety issue.  Hoi An is not even a legit UNESCO site anymore because today it exists solely to make money from tourists. It's just a money grab. It's essentially become a fake city.  When you see boat tours in the lake whereby there's so many boats that you're surrounded by them, you know it's just a money grab. These vloggers always tell you every place they visit is beautiful, amazing etc. and they only show you the good side, not the full side because all they care about is making money from scammy ad sales and scammy affiliate links.

Unfortunately, Vietnam does not know how to or care to practice sustainable tourism, so every place that gets popular is soon overrun by vendors who swarm the area and transform it into a S----show. The same thing has happened to Danang, Sapa, Ha Long Bay and Phu Quoc....totally s--shows.  Don't waste your time watching anyone who states otherwise. I wish the situation were different because I live in Vietnam, but it's not. And I have learned the hard way. Now I only travel to places in Vietnam that these ScamTubers aren't featuring which is why I'm not disclosing the names of those places (to keep them good).

text: I would say tips are expected in Vietnam now. For example, when you take a boat trip in Ninh Binh, the standard tip should be VND 50,000 VND~ 1.8$ for boat man. For cyclo, the tip should be VND 50,000 VND~ 1.8$ for cyclo drivers. Cyclo drivers in Hanoi and Hue may ask you directly for tipping which it's not nice in some cases. Thus, in order to avoid awkward situation, you can give tip right after services. It's a small amount when you consider the low income of the labour in Vietnam and how hard they work under the weather.

author: @nguyentandat2001
text:
As a Vietnamese person (ethnically Kinh), I want to speak frankly but respectfully to some foreign friends, especially Cham Muslims in Cambodia and parts of the Muslim community in Malaysia that claiming Cham heritage in Vietnam as “yours” lacks any serious academic basis. For most of its history, Champa was an Indianized kingdom, deeply shaped by Hinduism (Shaivism and Vaishnavism) and later Buddhism, with the Cham language belonging to the Austronesian family and a cultural identity distinct from the Malay–Islamic world.

In present-day Vietnam, the Cham community is officially recognized as having three main groups: Cham Bàlamôn (Ahiêr) and Cham Bàni (Awal), two long-established indigenous communities concentrated in Ninh Thuận and Bình Thuận, which are historically the heartland of Champa; and Cham Islam (orthodox Sunni), a later formation resulting from trade networks and Islamic missionary activities, mainly found in An Giang and parts of southern Vietnam. To attribute the entirety of Champa’s temples, art, religious practices, and customary laws to Islam or to “Malay culture” is a misrepresentation of history. Islam in the Cham context is a later layer of cultural adaptation, not the civilizational foundation of Champa. Mutual respect must begin with respect for historical facts: Champa’s heritage belongs to the Cham people, is preserved in Vietnam, and cannot be appropriated through oversimplified narratives or contemporary identity politics.

text:
I was quite interested in Vietnam history  before I travel to Vietnam recently. 
It may surprise many, but I believe the Campa people could have Indian or even Sri Lankan origins. In Sri Lanka, the worship of Lord Shiva dates back to very ancient times. Long ago, the Naga clan — one of the earliest known Sri Lankan communities — lived as skilled sea traders, connecting with many cultures around the world. Their symbol was the snake, which they proudly used as their emblem.

They were wealthy merchants who traded spices, pearls, gems, and metals. In ancient times, weaving was an important craft used to make clothing — something we also see in Cham culture. Even today, betel leaves and areca nut are used in auspicious events and when inviting priests, a tradition shared across many South and Southeast Asian cultures.

It is possible that one group of these prosperous sea merchants settled in a new land and eventually established their own kingdom. Later, with Chinese influence, their language, physical features, and cultural expressions may have evolved. However, ancestor worship is still practiced among many tribal communities, preserving a connection to the past.

No one can firmly claim a single origin, because the people of these regions are deeply mixed — influenced by Indian, Chinese, Arab, and later Western colonization. Original traditions naturally changed, and new traditions developed through these interactions. The same has happened to us in Sri Lanka. Some still argue about “pure origins,” without realizing that our own heritage has also been shaped by centuries of cultural exchange.

With globalization, cultures continue to change rapidly. The younger generation around the world often looks and lives similarly. Change is the ultimate reality. 😊❤

author: @Distancebetweenbyshubh
text:
A self-planned trip usually turns out cheaper, but you have to handle multiple bookings and plan the itinerary yourself. Lily’s services are good though, because I’ve taken packages from them twice. Even when the flight arrives early in the morning and the hotel doesn’t allow early check-in, they have a really nice office in Hanoi where you can freshen up.
The cost is higher mainly because they also have their profit margins. So, if you want more comfort and a smooth trip without the headache of managing different bookings, a package is a good option. Otherwise, if you feel you can make huge savings, you can definitely plan the trip on your own.

text: Hoi An to Pleiko is a LONG ride.   Good to see you got something to cover your arms from all the sun. Personally I prefer to cover shorter distances each day - like only 150km per day in Vietnam. In that area between Da Lat and Hoi An, there are some great coastal cities (Nha Trang, Tuy Hua, Quy Nhon) - which can be ridden to with very little time on Highway 1. And also another really great north-south route covering the northern 2/3 of Hoi An to Da Lat.. which is inland but closer to the coast than the western border. That path has mostly great road surfaces. On some sections, there are only small mountain cities, like Mang Den. But personally I liked Mang Den far better than Da Lat.

text:
Thanks for the video! There are some guide before visiting Bana:
- Prepare your health, bring a comfortable pair of shoes and bring as little belongings as possible, Bana is larger than you think and you will have to climb a lot.
- Plan the visit on sunny day, if you don't want to see nothing in the fog. I first visited Bana right at the cloudy day and it takes me another trip to see the true beauty of Bana.
- Even when the weather is nice, prepare a raincoat. Don't bring the umbrella, not very helpful because the wind in the highland is pretty strong, it could break the umbrella or make it useless.

author: @20luzer52
text:
Big fat thumbs up for your family to take the time to stop by Hue.  I think Hue is the most underrated city in Vietnam.  It's a city with a very unique pace and atmosphere and feel.  If you want to get away from the hectic pace of HCMC and Ha Noi, Hue is the place.  Cultured, low key and quiet people, not resort staff friendly but the subtle niceness of an old historic city.

I used to live and work in VN and my Vietnamese friends told me the people in Hue have the softest accent but the people there is the most principled and disciplined people in all of Vietnam.  

Back in 2002, I stopped in Hue and caught the Hue Festival, by chance, see the two high schools on Le Loi Boulevard ending and got to see hundreds of Vietnamese female students walk out of the gate in their traditional "ao dai" flowing and they looked like butterflies streaming out.  Saw couple of teenage boys on bicycles picking up their girlfriend on their bicycles and felt like I was in a novel.  I got a peek inside those high school school yard and was blown away by how beautiful those 2 high schools were.

video_title: AVOID These Tourist Scams in VIETNAM
author: @eds6535
text:
Good advice. My story combines this with your video about "don't visit Ha Long Bay". After research, I booked a overnight cruise on Ha Long Bay. The next day, she called and said they could "upgrade" us to a nicer ship. The other ship supposedly had some repairs that came up. I agreed. we got to Ha Long Bay, checked in and were told we were put onto an old boat, while others went to the boat I originally booked. I asked and they said I couldn't be changed. So I watched others get on the new ship in the photo, with jacuzzi, pool etc. We got on an old ship, maybe 40 years old. It was OK, but didn't have what I was promised. The other boat also had people taking out kayaks while we didn't. 
To top it off, they went to the main area of Ha Long Bay. 50 other boats, so no scenic photo ops. At night, booming music from the other boats took away any semblance of being out in nature or a World Heritage area. The cabin was OK and the crew nice, but certainly not the experience I expected. Plus my girlfriend, a Hanoi native who goes on these cruises often, was very disappointed with it. She even spoke to them, but they refused to put us on the other ship. It did anchor right near us and we could see it was full of what was obviously a large tour group, which I assume was why they changed us.
I appealed to them after for a refund and was ignored. Went back and appealed to Travelocity who did the booking and was told they had no control, no responsibility and could not get us a $338 refund. So I had to eat it. Very disappointed and yes, I consider it a scam! I didn't leave a bad review, I also heard what you mentioned about bad reviews and felt not only was it pointless, but didn't want issues with the government because of it.
Next time---Long Ha Bay. Sounds much better; and I think it may be more the wonderful natural area we wanted!

video_title: AVOID These Tourist Scams in VIETNAM
author: @dreaming-of-adventure
text:
Wow that’s such a great story! It’s so mean that they taunted you with the nicer ship the entire time! Was that the only scam you encountered in Vietnam? I definitely agree that it’s the classic bait and switch scam, even if it was just because they wanted to prioritize the big tour group. I’m surprised Travelocity didn’t do more for you. Did you try doing a chargeback for part of the cost, since you didn’t get what you paid for. If you paid through Travelocity they might just have passed that chargeback on to the tour company instead of trying to fight it on their behalf. 

Lots of people do leave reviews in Vietnam, locals as well, but it’s a weird situation when it comes to defamation laws. From what I’ve read if you stick to sharing your experience, you’re generally ok. Just don’t say they were terrible people or that you want them to go out of business. That could be construed as you wanting to harm the business, which would be defamation.

text:
Vietnamese people give me the impression of having a mentality very similar to what China was like about ten years ago: a strong sense of insecurity and inferiority, combined with the belief that they have somehow won every war they have fought. Even now, many of them still seem to believe that they “won” both the Vietnam War and the Sino-Vietnamese War. It feels like a kind of arrogance that grows out of insecurity.

Another thing is that when they look at their own culture, they often seem to deliberately ignore how much of it actually came from elsewhere. A large part of Vietnamese culture historically came from China, and many foods and cultural influences also came from China or France. Even much of what is considered traditional Vietnamese culture was heavily influenced by China, yet they often seem to intentionally downplay or ignore that connection.

There is also an excessive degree of nationalism. They act as though their country is exceptionally powerful or impressive, while forgetting that Vietnam is ultimately a relatively small and weak country in Southeast Asia. Many aspects of its political system, national traditions, and culture were influenced by or derived from other countries, and much of its modern civilization, industrialization, and modernization also came through outside influence.

What I find striking is this combination of insecurity and overconfidence: an almost baseless sense of superiority that seems to be produced by a deeper sense of inferiority.

author: @PervyK
text:
Brining usd seriously take it serioulsy when it comes to exchanging pristine new 100 bills. The smallest crease, blemish, and writing will seriously ding down its worth. a bengamin with a small defect will tank to 70-50% worth in exchange. A single fold makes it near worthless. It needs to be the most perfect bills you can find for good exchange.

For traveling to local places in the city - avoid the tourist traps where tourguides drop folks at. If you see alot of foreginers in a spot you are in the wrong spot to get any decent food for the local price. Travel down the street and you'll end up finding things 20-50% the price at higher quality and quantity sometimes because it snot stuff people know they can upsell for highest profit margins to foreigners who don't know what a good Pho or snack should taste like. 

Keep viet cash on you for when you gotta buy your way out of something. Bribing is just a thing over there. Don't give to much, dont cop a attitude or start a big commotion. You'll always lose. Obey the laws bc it'll be your hinny if they call you on it. 

Vietnam is extraordinarily safe. But petty theft like phone/wallet/bag snatching is still a thing as is any country. Just keep mind to have a iron grip. It really is a safe country though as long as you're not the one causing the problems.

Oh and dont drink the tap water, and only bottled/filtered. Eat nothing raw and cook that stuff good. The first few things you eat will dictate the rest fo your trip. Don't eat weird stuff and find yourself having diarrhea both ends. Acclimate a bit haha. Take it easy the first day or so.  Folks over there take pills for parasites occasionally for a reason. You may not be built for that off the boat.

text: Yes, it’s the same hotel. When you arrive, you first check in at the bottom station/reception, where you’ll also pay for both your room and the Bana Hills entry ticket. text: There are so many amazing coastal roads in Vietnam.  Hai Van is popular because most tourist are only in Da Nang for a few days.  So it is a quick & easy ride to do.  Wait until you do the North side, amazing rides there.

video_title: HAI VAN PASS: IS IT WORTH THE HYPE? 🇻🇳 Vietnam Motorbike Special - Top Gear | VIETNAM VLOG
author: @patnewman1
text: While I visited Vietnam in January 2020 I stayed in DaNang as a base but actually visited Hue and Phu Bai which were places that I served while in the US Army  101st Airborne Division. Because I visited those areas looking for certain things from my time while serving, I drove the Hai Van Pass 4 times round trip. It is one of the most fun rides that I have had because of the elevation and also the views of the coast are unbelievable. Seeing those pristine beaches were awe inspiring. Nice job again Gabi.

author: @carolineorner
text: I visited Hoi An in 2008 and it was immensely charming. It was not over crowded with tourists so the charm of the city was much more pronounced. I loved all of Vietnam and it became my favorite city in southeast Asia.

video_title: Anantara Hoi An Resort (Vietnam): impressions & review
author: @elizabethjackson2467
text:
My first stay was about 10 years ago when it was the Life Heritage Resort. It was far from perfect however their long stay package was excellent river view room, bfst, massages and airport pick up and drop of for $140 aud a night.  The massages still rate as some of the best that I have ever experienced. Beaten only by the Peninsula in Bangkok.
The hotel ended up being bought by the Anantara.  They dropped off all the included benefits and increased the rate.
We stopped staying when the rates went up to $300 aud with bfst.
The hotel is not 5*, 4* at the best.
Pros 
Lovely grounds
Attractive exterior
Close to Old Town
Cons
Far too expensive, much better for a third of the rate.
No lifts
Difficult to walk upstairs for breakfast for anyone with mobility issues.
Can be very noisy depending on the room.
Rooms are very dark
Rooms very dated
The rooms have recently been renovated so now maybe more attractive.

Frankly I do not understand why you have reviewed this hotel as a Luxury Resort as it is not.

I love Hoi An! It’s one of my favourite places in Vietnam! Although many tourists visit here, I like how no motorbike’s are allowed in the old town. If I ever move to Vietnam I would live here or Danang. 
The hotel looks a bit run down and not an Antatara luxurious as I thought. However, I do love the old charm of the French colonial designs. Credit to the architects thar designed these hotels. I was there in 2019 and staged in the Boutique hotel and it looked very similar to this hotel, just a bit out of town. I think if the pool was renovated it would be an amazing hotel. On my bucket list. 
Do you like this brand or Six Senses? I think Six Senses hotels are more remote and their signatures are their spa areas, really gorgeous settings. What are Thor thoughts as too have stayed in both?

author: @henrysing2782
text:
First of all thanks for your video view about my city. I am a local (currently living in Finland) and I am very beyond disatisfied about the video you make. There are few things I want to correct you in the video. 

1. The pollution you showed in the video, it was not true. It is foggy. Usually in the stormy day or even in the early morning, it can look like that but definitely not pollution. Da Nang is no way having pollution like that, compared to Beijing China, Beijing can look polluted like that but Da Nang will never be. Da Nang is surrounded by nature with jungle and sea/beach, that will not make it cloudly polluted like that. 

2. The sim card, I am sorry it happened everywhere, even in Europe. When you purchase something, better you know the service and you better ask local or get the review. Danang people are very honest and friendly but of course, there are some places they want to sell stuffs and trick customers of course, it happens everywhere in the world. To make sim card or internet, you can simply go to mobiphone or viettel stores to purchase it (same as Elisa or DNA in Finland). 

3. People cough and in our culture, it is allowed to cough and show it. We do not judge or look bad on them. 

Da Nang is no way perfect but it is a very enjoyable city with life-convenient-service that you will definitely not have it anywhere else. People are friendly and helpful, nature is all around and cost of living is affordable. AND definitely air quality will not be a problem to people, it is a generally a clean city. 

AND remember that, Vietnam has over 90 million people and do not compare it to small populated nations, of course it is more difficult to manage such a huge population and people are diversed. I hope you get my point. 

There are negative things about Da Nang ofc like any other cities in the world, but I hope the negative is really a negative, the difference is acceptable. Culture is different and custom is different too. I hope you respect my country and our custom. Thanks kiitos

author: @p0neh1
text:
This video was incredibly useful for when I was planning a trip to Vietnam in late August/Early September! We also went for 10 days. Me and two of my friends went to many of the places you listed in the video. We had originally planned to go to Sapa but I decided that Hoi An was the better option for the two days instead... and it was our favourite part of the trip too! We were there on National day, so it was very busy and there were lots of festivities in Hoi An! 

We went to Ha Long for two nights instead of one, which I think was a good option as we got a whole day cruise and experience on Cat Ba Island. We also got to kayak in some very quiet and intimate areas of the bay, where nobody but the three of us could be seen or heard and discovered the most beautiful hidden gem I have ever seen. I don't usually cry but... that little part of Ha Long we kayaked into was the most beautiful place I have ever seen. We also went to Ninh Binh and spent a bit longer in Hanoi than you did - went on a couple of motorbike tours around the city and nearby countryside. It was definitely a fun experience and this video helped me decide what we would do in the short time we spent in the country!

Yes, the image in English means ''Born to drift free” Similar to other familiar names the top-of-the-line electric motorcycle is the Vinfast Viper and when associated with Da Nang city and Hoi An ancient town creates a poetic parallel image. It reflects both the free-spiritedness of a young, modern city and the tranquil rhythm of an ancient heritage site.
- Modern Da Nang: A city of bridges, beaches, and a dynamic pace of life, always looking towards the future.
- Ancient Hoi An: An ancient town with lanterns, moss-covered tiled roofs, where memories and culture are preserved.
- The spirit of freedom: On one side, a constantly moving flow; on the other, a stillness that remains open to the world.
This combination makes the phrase “Born to drift free” a powerful and evocative message: both an invitation to tourists and an affirmation of the identity of this Central Vietnamese region I LOVE VIETNAM FORM DA NANG CITY AND HOI AN ANCIENT.

author: @amclarnon4102
text: My favorite was the entry officer didn't write a date at all.  I had no clue about the date.  The immigration officer who did the final check at the Cambodia border had an issue with the stamp and sent me and the bus lady back to the immigration officer.  He got mad and said it was fine and gave her back my passport.  The last officer shrugged his shoulders and let me through.  I was flying out to China for a visit when they sent me to a different counter where the officers said that I overstayed.  I showed them my evisa and when I told the officer what happened, he shocked his head and told the closest counter to let me go through.  He said neither officer should've let me through without a date for the entry stamp that was clearly in my passport underneath the Cambodia stamps.  Your video shows how important it is to check for the handwritten date if it is there and if it is correct.

author: @8BB88BB8
text: I've just finished a trip to Hanoi.  Actually it's very smooth at the immigration and customs if you've got everything prepared well before the trip, including but not limited to the application of a visa and filling in the immigration details within 72 hrs before the first day in Vietnam (indeed my QR code was not asked for upon getting through!), and checking correct of the details in the previously mentioned documents applied.  However, the overall experience of applying a visa gives me an impression that they're really many traps that visitors can easily fall prey to if not dealing with it cautiously.  Maybe it's kinda preparation for visiting Vietnam as we visitors should be very alert to stay away from scams everywhere in Vietnam (yet, Vietnam is generally very safe, but still, always be careful).

text: Please ensure you check what the legal monetary limits are (without declaring that is).  There is an amount for USD or foreign currency, and there is an amount for VND.  They are not the same.  USD5,000 is equivalent to VND130,000,000, but you are only allowed to travel (without declaring) VND15,000,000. Mr Duong did say in his video that it was VND130M, whereas the background/embedded subtitle says VND15M (at approx. 05:40).  I did find out the hard way on exiting the country, not on entering the country.  While it wasn't fun spending time with security officers in a small side room, they were very polite and walked through the rules and regulation.  Like Mr Duong says, check your situation as things can change, and you don't want to get caught doing something wrong by mistake.  Enjoy your travels.

text: It is my understanding that having a confirmed exit flight is not a condition for the issuance of a visa. You just need to depart before the expiry date. A lot of back packers take a bus from Saigon to Cambodia and  more richer tourists take an expensive ferry tour up the Mekong to PP. author: @davidgiffen6349
text: @heythave  my mother would have turned eighty two the week she died.  My parents traveled together until my father died twelve years prior to my mother’s death.  They didn’t go to Vietnam while he was alive because he thought there were no hotels that were nice enough for my mother. He was so protective that he didn’t really acknowledge her adventurous spirit. They were among the first people to tour in China after Nixon went there.  The hotels were terrible.  Russian built, in a way the Chinese had no idea how to maintain. Their group actually took food with them because there were no restaurants in areas they were allowed to go to as the first tourists.  People in rural areas, held their children up to see my parents as they went by.  My parents were quite tall and my father had bright blue eyes with extremely bushy blond eyebrows.

author: @StevenSmith-ob8yq
text: It is hard to go wrong in Vietnam, but I would like to offer a different spin on lodging.  My theory is that luxury lodging distances me from regular people in my destination.  In 2013 I visited Vietnam for the first time.  I chose a reasonably low-priced homestay (I would describe it as a small hotel which provides close personal service).  $20 per night included breakfast, as well as dinner most nights.  Also free were coffee, fruit juices, and fruit all day.  The crazy thing is that the owner invited my daughter and me to go up to her home village north of Hanoi on a day trip.   I'm heading to Vietnam in about 10 days for a 90+ day visit with side trips most likely to Siem Reap, Japan, and Taiwan.

text: Sujith Bro, Ho Chi Minh City is very famous for street food. But you should very careful in selecting food items. Shell fish is most dangerous food stuff if not properly cooked. There are good Indian restaurants in Ho Chi Minh City where you will get all sorts of  North Indian food. Nite life is very vibrant, but should be careful in selecting pubs.  Vietnam is a developing country and snooty traffic is famous as you could see in all major traffic areas. You could see the reminents of Vietnam war, while southern Vietnam is supported by USA while northern area was controlled by Russian army. Hanoi and Danang are the places to visit of tourists importance. I have visited most of the places in Vietnam for few times for official tours. Looking forward to hear more from you on Vietnam. Hi Sujith, the Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh's body is on display in this mausoleum & historic site in Hanoi. Please try not to miss it when you are in Hanoi. There's strict rules before entering to meet the legendary "Uncle Ho".

Hanoi is an administrative city and is a very subdued city as compared with HCM city, which is more hot and happening.

Happy to see HCM city (bikes city) thru your lens and maybe later of Hanoi, the 2 Vietnamese cities I last visited 2 months ago. 

Being a heavily populated bike city, please be careful with your phone/camera while shooting from city pavements.  I am always closely guarded by my local staff when I am walking on the pavements and roadside.

author: @NguyenDuyKhanh02
text:
Là một người Việt Nam tôi có thể khẳng định rằng những món ăn đường phố đều ngon hơn nhà hàng. Đây không phải điều vô lý sau khi bạn biết rằng những phố phường và khu chợ là nơi hình thành nên văn hoá, truyền thống. Người Việt xưa thường đi chợ vào sáng sớm để chuẩn bị bữa ăn, những người bán hàng cũng sẽ dậy từ rất sớm để chuẩn bị cho gian hàng vì vậy nên buổi sáng sẽ rất tấp lập. Sau khi đi về từ khu chợ ,thông thường họ sẽ tập thể dục lúc 6 giờ sáng và 6 chiều, bạn sẽ thấy khung cảnh rất nhiều ở công viên và bãi biển. Không khí chợ sáng sớm và không khí đón bình minh rất tuyệt vời, tôi nghĩ bạn nên thử nó. Một điều khác tôi muốn nói là khi chọn quán ăn, thay vì chọn chỗ du lịch và có đông người du lịch thì hãy tìm chỗ có nhiều người địa phương tìm đến, nó rẻ hơn và ngon hơn. Nhưng đừng chọn quán ăn có giá thấp hơn so với các quán ăn xung quanh, nếu tốt nhất thì hãy hỏi những người địa phương

Một điều thú vị nữa là "cà phê trứng" được tạo ra trong khoảng thời gian thiếu thốn nguyên liệu, họ cho lòng đỏ trứng vào cà phê để thay cho sữa đặc khan hiếm

text:
One of the best meal I ever had was in a dirty Central Highlands city called Kontum.  At about 5am, I pulled my motorbike over and bought a sandwich from an early-opening stand.  The vender’s English was as negligible as my Vietnamese so I just pointed to one of the sandwiches already made.
It was really delicious: creamy and rich and oddly sweet — and tantalizingly familiar.  After a few bites, I cracked it open: the filling was... granulated sugar and butter.
Now, I cannot recommend this dish as an actual food, but at that moment, jet-lagged, sleep-deprived, isolated, my body needed exactly that.

text: Don’t believe all of these fake social media influencers and lying YouTube posts who make Vietnam look like the hot new paradise on earth because it isn’t.  Just went to visit Vietnam and check it out and it’s a 6 out of 10.  Thailand is much better 9/10 for many reasons like much better infrastructure, the politeness of the local Thai people.  In Vietnam the vibe is more aggressive & rude like back in America and the language barrier is worse than you think so you can’t communicate with the people.  Plus the big elephant sitting in the living room is the stigma of the horrible Vietnam war dead ghosts still hangs where 58,000 Americans died and 3 million Vietnamese died gives it a weird paranormal feeling.  Reminded me of the killing fields of Cambodia with pol pot who killed 3 million of his own people or visiting world war 2 battlefields in Europe where millions were murdered with the same weird ghost paranormal feelings.  In Vietnam it was a constant surreal experience & feeling to think that my uncle fought only 49 miles from our beach front resort in Da Nang in one of the bloodiest battles of the Vietnam war where thousand perished in bloody door to door combat.  I couldn’t stop thinking about it and remembering his stories of almost being killed by a booby trap bomb toy bear he picked up and exploded in his face placed by the enemy.

author: @quyenoan5320
text:
Really really nice video! I can see the dedication you put in for every shot and the effort to speak and write the vietnamese name of each dish. Thank you so much! It's just that I cant help myself correcting some details:
1:47 The "phở cá" that you mentioned is actually a very different and not a common dish, definitely not the same "bún cá" that you were having, even though "phở" and "bún" are both types of rice noodle, the soups that are paired with them usually have very different and distinctive flavour, hardly interchangeable. The vegetable is probably water crust or some similar sort as I have never seen morning glory go with this dish before. And you are absolutely right about "bún cá" being a good refreshing hangover soup, the youngsters ate it a lot during the Lunar New Year Holiday after all the repetitive heavy traditional meals. 
5:06 Here in the North, "chả giò" is usually called "nem rán" (literal translation is fried meat roll) 
6:22 I'm not quite sure about the yellow skin indicating that it's aged chicken because normally "phở" is preferably prepared with fresh chicken. And the boiled chicken skin we have here is always that yellow. 
6:53 8:02 You got the translation for "nộm thịt bò khô" quite correct but the word for "salad" here is "nộm" while "thịt bò khô" is "dried beef" or "beef jerky"
9:01 "Chè" is actually a broad term for many of different types of sweet pudding soup we have here and even though "chè khúc bạch" is the name of the shop, I believe what you had there was a different type of "chè" as the "khúc bạch" one is flavoured milk jellies that are eaten with thin lychee flavoured syrup and topped with lychee and almond slices. (Personally really love it myself) 
10:59 "Bánh tráng cuốn" (without the ending "g") is actually rolled rice paper and it should be "bánh tráng nướng" - fried rice paper that you were showing.
13:24 The higher price for public holidays is a way that businesses try to pay the employees that sacrify their days off to work, quite common here. 
14:33 The spatula is actually a single giant thin chopstick. In addition I doubt that the meat must be pork and not beef, never seen it in typical "bánh cuốn" to be honest. The cinnamon note is obvious because that type of ham is purposely made with the cinnamon flavor (the orange part). It's called "chả quế" - cinnamon ham. 
18:16 The "riêu" is actually crab paste as we would crush/pound whole small sweet-water crabs and gently boil it to get that airy crumbly cake texture.
28:14 We can let go of the other mispelling but definitely not this one because of the meaning of that word 😅 The one you want to put there is "Phở bò". I guess that you pick up the "Cơm Phở" from the vendor's sign but it just read as "rice and phở". Fun fact is that many vietnamese vendors dont really have a name and just put up name of the dishes that they are selling. 
28:24 We dont use chives for phở, that's actually spring onions
30:45 They're pickled papayas and carrots, other places might put them on the side for you to put in based on your preference. 32:00 Yes, bún chả is supposed to be served warm, perfect for the cold winter of Hanoi. Love how your mother did a ssam for you there. 
36:50 The "nem chua rán" is actually made of pork and pork skin, which explains the jelly chewy texture. The black sause tho, I think it's a mixture of soy sauce (maggi or other brand) and tamarind as we call it tamarind sauce - "sốt me"
42:40 The typical filling should be green beans. Most types of nuts except for peanuts are quite expensive ingredient in Vietnam so the most popular filling for so many  traditional cakes and sweets is bean, expecially green bean. 
Lastly, it's so cute  each time you said fish sauce in vietnamese but it should be nước "mắm" with an "m" ^^
Of course my notes are not absolute as the culture and cuisine of Vietnam are very diverse and there are a lot of variations of each dish among regions. Just an urge to share a more indigenous view. Again, thank you so much for making such a nice video introducing Vietnamese with your culinary insight, Tina. Glad your family had fun!

author: @k3ntr1l
text:
Hello Tina! Congrats on your trip to Vietnam and Hanoi! I’m honestly more proud than I should be to have you visit my city lol😭 but anyways. I do want to add some extra notes to the foods you featured here:
- I wouldn’t describe it as fish pho personally, bún cá feels very much like its own thing. 
- Regarding the place where you ate both the phở gà and the bún chả, from my experience, restaurants that covers many different types of foods usually can not match with a restaurant who specializes in that food. So the bún chả having the chả (which is the meat) being a little dry is honestly kind of expected😭
- Actually, the papaya salad you ate is actually called nộm, while the “bò khô” is actually beef jerky, and the fish sauce should be called nước mắm, with an “mmm” sound at the beginning of the second word
- The Bánh Mỳ Phố is actually a chain of bánh mỳ, and personally, independent vendors will generally always have better quality 
- I love you so much for covering bánh cuốn!! It’s always seemed very underrated to me as a dush
- I actually think you going on Lunar New Year was a disadvantage, because everyone will close their business on New Years (understandably so) so it might have hindered your food experiences a little bit
- Riêu would be more closely translated as crab butter in English, and the combination of bún riêu and bún ốc would be bún riêu ốc
- Very glad you tried out Grab, it’s just so iconic to Vietnamese transportation
- Nem chua rán is such an iconic snack, and it’s actually made by fermenting raw pork until it develops a sour smell, which is the “chua” part
Again, thank you so much for visiting our country and city, and producing a beautiful video to accompany it🩷🩷

author: @visa2explore
text:
Harish Bali this side, looking at comments i spotted this trail, so thought to write a comment here... I agree with your thoughts on this subject. 

We are mostly running short of time bcoz things on the ground are not as easy at it seems, so much of time gets consumed in taking permission for making video at respective place. This is background of the food. My team does not prefer local food unless i push them to have it in lunch or dinner. 

I try to motivate them but if they say they want to have indian food then, no second time asking, i go with them to indian food restaurant. When you go to any restaurant it takes times , if after they are done with their food, i decide that i want to go to local food eatery then you lose your time badly.....This is one reason.

Most youtubers travel on their own  without any team, which somehow i can't do, my dependence is on them for video shoot, so i have to be 100% flexible when it comes to food choice preference. Plus they are pure veg, don't even eat egg.... so we decided that atleast one meal of the day we will have in Indian food. Now the option which is left is shoot or ignore.. 

if i had cut this indian food option from the video, then there would be no trail here, that's how things are....Most of us generally pin point what we don't like in a particular video and in many cases miss to mention what was good or alteast  better then many other videos available online on that very subject.

My personal preference is so much towards local food and culture that learning about it and sharing through video is my first preference but sometimes bcoz of reasons beyond control, things are not always aligned to the objective, despite best efforts.

Rest all good, BTW - Central Vietnam is the most beautiful place of Vietnam. Bye for now.

- *Duration:* 15 days

- *Accommodation:* We prefer comfortable 4- to 5-star hotels.
- *Ha Long Bay:* We would love to experience an overnight luxury cruise.
- *Phu Quoc:* We definitely want to include Phu Quoc in our itinerary.
- *Interests:* We love beautiful landscapes, beaches, islands, scenic places, local food, unique experiences, cable cars, and relaxing activities suitable for the whole family.
- *Not interested in:* Historical sites, museums, and history-focused sightseeing.
- *Travel style:* We prefer a relaxed and comfortable holiday rather than a hectic schedule with too much travelling.

Could you please prepare a detailed itinerary covering the best destinations for us, including how many nights to spend at each place, suggested hotels, internal flights and transfers, activities, sightseeing, restaurant recommendations, and an approximate overall budget for our family?

We would especially appreciate your advice on how best to combine *Phu Quoc, Ha Long Bay, and the other must-visit destinations in Vietnam within 15 days* without making the trip too tiring for the children.

Please let me know if you offer personalised itinerary-planning services and what your charges would be.

Thank you for creating such informative and inspiring travel content. I look forward to hearing from you!

Warm regards,  
Vaibhav Buty

I want to discover this additional secret when I return to Da Nang next year --> unless of course you discover it first :>))

text:
Kelly is a great wife and mom for being how patient she is throughout the filming process.
As for the variety of bananas, I recall VN have so many different types.  I would think Indonesia (I believe you live and work in Indonesia ?!?!?) would be the same.  I remember VN bananas are very fragrant, and those bananas have a long shelf life even as ripe bananas.  Even if the skin had gone dark for a long time, the inside is still abit spongy/chewy and is still good and doesn't go bad like Chiquita bananas we have here in the US.
The other thing I  noticed is that the bananas in VN are very very fragrant.  I had moved back to the US for 10 yrs now and don't smell the fragrance of the bananas we have here even if they are ripe.
They are smaller too, kind of cute actually.
Hope you guys are enjoying yourselves and will be able to get the kids to do some fun things like water park or the beach.

Thank you for visiting our country. But I want to say a few things that foreign friends still misunderstand about Vietnam. First, Vietnamese people are not like Chinese people. Thankyou so much for bringing back such happy memories of my visit to Hue I really loved that combination of Vietnamese and French colonial style.I want to go back to visit the famous college there,visit the centre near the Imperial City run by people with mental disabilities (it sounds amazing especially as I work in this sector here in London UK) and at the city centre hotel where I stayed they had a scheme where hotel guests could volunteer to spend a few hours of their stay helping poor Vietnamese students with their English language.Sadly I only discovered this on my last day but I vowed to return as I felt it was a wonderful idea by the hotel manager.Sadly this damn virus situation as spoiled my plans but I am trying to remain patient.Being British I thought I might be able to help a few students with the mother tongue.Did you have a chance to visit Europe it's such a wonderful continent...nearly as lovely as Asia!And finally dear yes you must visit lovely Japan.The people are so polite and the service you receive everywhere is wonderful definitely no scams....and the trains run exactly to time ha not like here!!! I still remember those hot Vietnamese Summer days I love warm weather but even for me it was hot hot hot!!
With Blessings for your day.Steve

author: @quocnguyenngoc9272
text: Of the Nguyen tombs, I prefer by far the tomb of Gia Long, the founder of the Nguyen dynasty. There is a bridge now so you can go there by road. I hired a boat (as the bridge was not finished then) and took "xe ôm" to go from the river banks to the tomb complex. It is quite a way out. On the way back, I hired a Ca Huế troupe (who came to the boat) to listen to traditional music on the Perfume river, a very pleasant experience. I should point out that the Nón Lá (the conical hat) nowadays is a lot smaller than the old design. The larger hat looks much better. You can still see women with the older, larger hats in the Northern highlands. In Huế, it should be nón bài thơ.
